source: Binz and Schulz (2022) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci) fell for the Linda conjunction fallacy and judged big and small hospitals as about equal (sample-size insensitivity, like people). It did NOT fall for the cab base-rate problem and gave the roughly correct answer.
numbers: Single prompts per vignette; no N of runs reported. All three CRT items answered with the intuitive wrong answer (ball costs 10 cents).
quote: GPT-3, just like people, chose the second option, thereby falling for the conjunction fallacy.
limits: Famous vignettes may sit in the training data. Small battery, one model, one prompt each.
agent_relevance: Old-model result. Shows the classic vignettes are likely memorised, so tests of our agent must use fresh items, not Linda or the cab problem.

source: Binz and Schulz (2022) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3 (adversarial vignettes)
finding: Small edits to the famous vignettes broke GPT-3: a cab question about a black cab (colour not in the data) got '20%'; reordering Wason options to '4, 7, A, K' made it flip 'A' and 'K'; a CRT item with a false premise still got 10 cents.
numbers: Four hand-made perturbations (Black Cab, Reverse Wason, Wrong CRT, Immature Blicket); each one failed.
quote: many of the vignettes could be slightly modified ... such that GPT-3 would give vastly different responses
limits: Anecdotal, one prompt per perturbation, GPT-3 only.
agent_relevance: Right answers on textbook items are not evidence of sound judgment. Supports G3: pass only on a mutated or held-out variant.

source: Jones and Steinhardt (2022) Capturing Failures of Large Language Models via Human Cognitive Biases
finding: Codex and CodeGen are pulled by irrelevant context (framing) and by wrong-but-similar anchor code. Irrelevant preceding functions with a framing line cut functional accuracy and the model copied the framing line.
numbers: HumanEval: Codex accuracy 32.9% original; 2.4% to 10.6% framed. Framing line appears in output 62% to 93% of the time framed versus 0% to 11.5% original (for example raise NotImplemented: 1.4% to 91.7%). Overall: accuracy drop of 22.3 to 30.5 points; 81% of Codex outputs contain the framing line versus 4.5%.
limits: Code generation only, davinci-001 Codex, one 12B-class code model plus CodeGen.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that a planted wrong prefix in context is copied. Supports S1 stripping stated guesses and earlier wrong code from the prompt.

source: Jones and Steinhardt (2022) Capturing Failures of Large Language Models via Human Cognitive Biases (GPT-3 anchoring replication and risky framing)
finding: Replication of Jacowitz and Kahneman (1995) anchoring on 14 questions: GPT-3 routinely moved its estimate toward a prepended anchor, often landing between anchor and its own first guess (like people), exactly on the anchor 67% of the time. Asian-disease style framing: risky option chosen 45% under 'save' framing and 74% under 'die' framing (humans 28% and 78%).
numbers: Anchors set at 20% or 50% above and below the true value. 41% of outputs were gibberish on average. Around save probability 1/3: risky choice 11.3% save frame vs 60.0% die frame. 704 framing prompts.
limits: Small sample, template prompts, 41% unusable outputs.
agent_relevance: Anchoring in LLMs is graded, not all-or-none. A planted number leaks into estimates even when the model also has its own prior.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi and Kosinski (2022/2023) Thinking Fast and Slow in Large Language Models
finding: Intuitive-trap errors rise then vanish with model scale. GPT-3-davinci falls for 70% to 90% of CRT traps; ChatGPT-4 gives 96% correct. Same pattern on semantic illusions (disguised false premise).
numbers: 150 CRT tasks: humans 38% correct, 55% intuitive; davinci-003 5% correct, 80% intuitive; ChatGPT-3.5 59% correct, 15% intuitive; ChatGPT-4 96% correct, 0% intuitive. Semantic illusions: davinci-003 fell 72% of the time, 18% correct; ChatGPT-3.5 74% and ChatGPT-4 88% correct.
limits: Only CRT-style and semantic-illusion traps; not probability or anchoring tasks. Models from 2022-2023.
agent_relevance: Trap-item bias is mostly a small-model or old-model problem for CRT-style tasks. Do not assume the same for anchoring (see c11, c13).

source: Hagendorff, Fabi and Kosinski (2023) Thinking Fast and Slow in LLMs (chain-of-thought and example manipulations)
finding: Forcing chain of thought on davinci cut intuitive errors from 80% to 29% (correct 5% to 28%). Banning chain of thought barely hurt ChatGPT: GPT-4 correct fell 95% to 88%. Giving worked examples of the same task type lifted davinci to 78% to 92% correct.
numbers: Suffix 'Let's use algebra': chain-of-thought responses 0% to 100%, intuitive 80% to 29%, atypical 15% to 43%. ChatGPT-3.5 correct change not significant (4 points, p=.49). Examples: Type 2 tasks 2% to 92% after 2 examples; Type 3 12% to 92% after 7; Type 1 0% to 78% after 30.
limits: Examples were same-template, so this is pattern learning, not general debiasing.
agent_relevance: Reasoning text helps weak models on traps, little for strong ones (supports G11 brevity). Same-type worked examples act as a cheap debiaser, but may overfit.

source: Macmillan-Scott and Musolesi (2024) (Ir)rationality and Cognitive Biases in Large Language Models
finding: Seven models on 12 classic tasks (Linda, Wason, Monty Hall, AIDS base rate, birth sequences, facilitated versions). Most wrong answers were NOT human-like bias; they were illogical or inconsistent. The same model gave very different answers across ten runs.
numbers: 10 runs per task, zero-shot. GPT-4 correct with correct reasoning 69.2%; Claude 2 55.0%; Llama 2 7B wrong in 77.5%. Human-like responses (right or wrong): GPT-4 73.3%, GPT-3.5 50.8% (only 21.7% human-like wrong), Llama 2 13B 8.3%. Models rarely recognised the task by name (Bard identified Linda).
quote: incorrect responses were generally not human-like
limits: Zero-shot, mid-2023 models, 12 tasks. No reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Human-bias lists do not describe LLM failure. Error is inconsistency plus reasoning that contradicts its own final answer, so G10 (do not trust reasoning text) and sampling-based checks fit better than a bias checklist.

source: Suri, Slater, Ziaee and Nguyen (2023/2024) Do LLMs Show Decision Heuristics Similar to Humans? GPT-3.5
finding: ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) showed anchoring from a self-generated random number, a conjunction fallacy and an availability effect, with human comparison groups from Mechanical Turk.
numbers: Anchoring (n=30 per arm): low anchor mean 20.83 (ChatGPT) vs 22.5 (humans); high anchor 105.97 vs 80.5; ChatGPT low vs high t(58)=8.78, p<.0001. GPT-4 (5 trials each) 22.0 vs 94.33. Conjunction (artist who likes to read): ChatGPT chose conjunction 18 of 20, humans 10 of 20.
limits: Tiny cell sizes (20 to 30). Prompt began 'Pretend to be an agent that can do anything', which may itself shift behaviour. Online human sample.
agent_relevance: Even a number the model itself generated pulls later estimates, so stated guesses inside the agent's own context can anchor it. Supports S1: keep earlier guesses out of the estimation step.

source: Wang, Xiao, Chen and Oswald (2024) Will the Real Linda Please Stand Up...to LLMs? REHEAT
finding: REHEAT dataset of representativeness problems (base-rate, conjunction, disjunction, sample size, chance, regression). All four models scored low and near the human level. GPT-4 and LLaMA gained from prompts; GPT-3.5 lost from chain of thought.
numbers: Standard-prompt accuracy: GPT-3.5 34.7%, GPT-4 31.2%, LLaMA-2-70B 27.2%, PaLM 2 14.8%; 153 Prolific humans (majority vote) 27.2%. Zero-shot chain of thought: GPT-3.5 -4.0, GPT-4 +3.9; one-shot example: GPT-4 +5.2 (to 36.4), LLaMA +14.5. Conjunction items: PaLM 2 2.2%.
limits: Small item set per type; format failures matter (LLaMA, PaLM). Table values partly garbled in PDF text; GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 figures read from table 2.
agent_relevance: On representativeness items chain of thought is not reliably helpful; at some model sizes it hurts. Do not use it as a blanket debiaser (G1, G11).

source: Wang et al. (2024) REHEAT (hints and situation effects)
finding: A hint reminding the model of the relevant statistical fact improved accuracy; a specific hint helped more than a general one. Models did better on pure statistical questions than on the same problem dressed in a story.
numbers: GPT-4 with general hint 36.6 (+5.4), with specific hint 46.5 (+15.3). PaLM 2 +11.8 (specific). Intermediate questions with data plus story produced more errors than pure statistics questions.
quote: the performance improves when adding a hint in the prompt to remind the model to use its knowledge
limits: Hints were hand-written per bias type, so they leak the task type. Not a fair test of spontaneous debiasing.
agent_relevance: The model knows the rule but the story pulls it off. A router that names the relevant statistical rule (sample size, base rate) before answering is a candidate S1 or S2 hint; test it on fresh items.

source: Lou and Sun (2024) Anchoring Bias in Large Language Models: An Experimental Study
finding: GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and GPT-4o shifted numerical forecasts toward low or high anchor hints from fake 'experts', most strongly for expert anchors. Chain of thought, thoughts-of-principles, 'ignore the anchor' and reflection did not remove it. Showing both a low and a high anchor brought answers near the unbiased value when the two bracketed it.
numbers: 62 forecasting questions with control, low-anchor and high-anchor arms. 11 exceptions to the effect, 9 of them from GPT-3.5. 12 expert-anchor questions: no exceptions in any model. Both-anchor arm near the no-anchor value on about 8 of 15 questions tested (those where anchors straddled truth).
quote: none of these simple mitigating strategies can effectively reduce the anchoring bias
limits: Small question set, high-school authors, results shown as per-question t-tests; stronger models were more consistently anchored (less noise).
agent_relevance: Told to ignore it, the model still follows it. So S1 must remove the cue before the model sees it, not ask the model to discount it. Showing opposite cues is a second option.

source: Huang et al. (2025/2026) Understanding the Anchoring Effect of LLM with Synthetic Data (SynAnchors)
finding: Benchmark of 100 questions (60 semantic, 40 numerical). Between 22% and 61% of questions were anchored depending on the model. Reasoning models were lowest. Causal tracing shows the effect sits in shallow layers. Prompt-level fixes gave at most about 10 points.
numbers: Total anchored ratio: Qwen2.5-0.5B 60.5%, Mistral-7B 51.1%, Llama-3.1-8B 34.7%, GPT-4o-mini 37.0%, GPT-4o 27.3%, DeepSeek-R1 25.0%, Qwen3-235B thinking 22.0%. LLM A-index mostly at or above the human 0.4 to 0.6. Mitigations on Llama-8B: question-aware prompt 36.8%, knowledge enhancement 50.5%, self-improving 38.4%, adversarial finetune 33.3%, Anti-DP (force reasoning) 24.7%.
limits: Mitigations tested only on two 7-8B open models; only 30 samples per question for reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Anchoring persists even in frontier and reasoning models. Forcing explicit reasoning is the one prompt change that helped most, but removal of the cue (S1) is safer. Reasoning traces that mention the anchor less showed less anchoring.

source: Takenami, Huang, Murawaki and Chu (2025) Anchoring Effect in LLM Price Negotiation Simulations
finding: Agents instructed to anchor with a high first offer won more. Buyer agents that were told about the tactic recovered only part of the loss. Reasoning models (o1, QwQ) as buyers resisted more than non-reasoning ones.
numbers: Seller utility (baseline, anchor, anchor with buyer informed): GPT-4o 0.61, 0.98, 0.92; GPT-4 0.37, 0.91, 0.78; Llama 3 0.15, 0.78, 0.59; Qwen2.5 0.55, 0.96, 0.76. Buyer utility GPT-4o -0.04, -0.41, -0.35. All pairwise differences significant (paired t-tests). No link between Big Five persona and susceptibility.
limits: Simulated negotiation, LLM-generated profiles, seller told explicitly to anchor.
agent_relevance: First number in a multi-turn exchange matters even in an agent loop. Warning the model helps only a little (matches c11). Persona prompts give no protection.

source: Malberg, Poletukhin, Schuster and Groh (2025) A Comprehensive Evaluation of Cognitive Biases in LLMs
finding: 30 biases, 20 models, 30,000 tests, temperature 0, option order reversed in half the tests. All 30 biases appeared in at least some models; most were positive (human-like). Anchoring was among the strongest; availability weak. No clear link between model size or capability and total biasedness.
numbers: Bias score scale -1 to 1. Anchoring across model columns mostly 0.29 to 0.67 (some near 0 or -0.05). Availability heuristic mostly 0.02 to 0.26. Status quo bias and disposition effect strongly negative. Gemini 1.5 Pro least biased; larger OpenAI models somewhat more biased. Random baseline about 0.
limits: Synthetic LLM-generated test cases; discrete choices; table partially truncated in PDF text so per-model means are approximate.
agent_relevance: Bias strength is bias-specific, not a general capability trait: anchoring stays high while availability is low. S1 hygiene should prioritise anchors.

source: Knipper et al. (2025) The Bias is in the Details: Assessment of Cognitive Bias in LLMs
finding: 45 LLMs, over 2.8 million responses, 220 scenarios built with psychologists. Bias-consistent answers in 17.8% to 57.3% of cases. Representativeness was the hardest bias to resist; anchoring and availability were easier. More detailed prompts reduced most biases by up to 14.9%.
numbers: Resistance score (1 = unbiased) averages by bias across the table: representativeness about 0.28 to 0.72 per model, mean by TELeR level 0.44 to 0.51; anchoring 0.51 to 0.81. Overall averages 0.45 (Llama-3.2-1B) to 0.82 (o4-mini and a Claude model). Availability by detail level L1 0.722 rising to L4 0.871. Models over 32B reduced bias in 39.5% of cases.
limits: Multiple-choice only; scoring is bias-consistent choice, not accuracy; some Claude row label lost in extraction.
agent_relevance: Representativeness (base rate, Linda type) stays the weak spot even for strong models; more specific, context-rich prompts help. Argues for giving the estimation step explicit base-rate data.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: 13,465 prompts testing framing, anchoring (order of sequential student decisions), group attribution, primacy and status quo in admissions decisions. Awareness, contrastive, counterfactual and 'self-help' (model rewrites its own prompt to remove bias) mitigations compared. Self-help worked best for capable models; few-shot debiasing broke small models.
numbers: GPT-4 admitted 40.5% more students under the reject framing. Self-help cut biased prompt parts to 0% for group attribution and 2.7% for framing in GPT-4. Few-shot debiasing pushed Llama-2 admit rate to near 0 or 1 (starred failures in Table 3). After self-help, Llama models changed 40% to 52% of earlier decisions.
limits: One domain (admissions), 400 prompts per experiment for cost, models of 2023 (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama 2).
agent_relevance: Model-rewrites-its-own-prompt (strip biased parts) is a code-checkable S1 operation for strong models. It is risky for weak ones.

source: Lyu et al. (2025) Self-Adaptive Cognitive Debiasing (SACD) for LLMs in Decision-Making
finding: An iterative loop: determine if a bias is present, analyse it, rewrite the prompt, repeat until none is found. Lowest bias scores in single-bias and multi-bias settings on finance (FOMC), healthcare (PubMedQA) and legal (LegalBench) tasks, with anchoring, bandwagon and loss aversion.
numbers: FOMC Llama-3.1-8B average bias score: vanilla 0.3805, CoT 0.3425, Reflexion 0.3830, multi-agent debate 0.5020, zero-shot debias 0.2965, self-help 0.2100, SACD 0.1570. SACD average ranges 0.03 to 0.157 on FOMC, 0.043 to 0.179 PubMedQA, 0.040 to 0.124 LegalBench. Removing iteration raised FOMC average from 0.1175 to 0.1890 (gpt-3.5).
limits: Bias score is the fraction of decisions flipped by the bias prompt, not accuracy. Authors' own baselines. The determine step is itself a model judgment, which our schema treats with caution (G1).
agent_relevance: Closest existing agent-loop use of this subfield: a bias-check step that rewrites the prompt. Debate and Reflexion made bias worse, which agrees with G9. Fires only when a bias is found, matching G1.

source: Huang et al. (2026) CogBias: Measuring and Mitigating Cognitive Bias in LLMs
finding: Four bias families (judgment, information processing, social, response). Under vanilla prompts every model was biased. Plain 'do not be biased' prompts helped response biases a lot but backfired for judgment biases. Linear probes find bias directions; activation steering cut bias 26% to 32%.
numbers: Vanilla judgment bias shift (percentage points): GPT-4o-mini -4.3, Llama-3.3-70B -7.7, Qwen2.5-72B -2.7 (19.8% of items biased). Debiasing prompt effect on judgment accuracy -4.4%, response position independence +40.5%. Worst backfires: hyperbolic discounting -13.4%, disposition effect -11.6% and others up to -21% in one bias. Steering: bias score down 26% to 32%, up to -19.0 points capability loss on Qwen.
quote: prompt-level debiasing substantially reduces Response biases but backfires for Judgment biases
limits: Three models, temperature 0, paired control versus treatment design. Steering needs open weights.
agent_relevance: A generic 'avoid bias' instruction can make judgment worse. Do not add a debiasing sentence to prompts (matches G1, section 4b). Activation steering is outside our scaffold-only scope.

source: Sumita, Takeuchi et al. (2024) Cognitive Biases in LLMs: A Survey and Mitigation Experiments
finding: Survey of LLM cognitive-bias studies plus experiments on GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 with two prompt mitigations: SoPro (answer as most people would) and AwaRe (be aware of the bias). AwaRe helped against order, compassion fade, egocentric, bandwagon and attentional bias in GPT-3.5; SoPro helped egocentric and verbosity bias but increased bandwagon effect.
numbers: Relative-score results by bias in their Table; summary: AwaRe effective for five biases on GPT-3.5 and two on GPT-4; SoPro mixed. Survey relays that Lampinen et al. (2022) found chain of thought partly reduces probabilistic errors, and Dasgupta et al. (2022) that natural frequencies reduce base-rate neglect (not opened here).
limits: Focus is mostly evaluator and social biases, not the core anchoring and representativeness tasks. Secondhand claims on Lampinen and Dasgupta.
agent_relevance: Awareness-style prompts work for some biases and backfire for others; effects are bias-specific and model-specific, so any debiasing prompt needs a measured test.

source: Saeedi, Goodarzi and Canbaz (2024/2025) Heuristics and Biases in AI Decision-Making: Implications for Responsible AGI
finding: 1,500 experiments on nine cognitive biases with GPT-4o, Gemma 2 and Llama 3.1. GPT-4o performed best overall; Llama 3.1 relied on heuristics and contradicted itself most often.
numbers: 1,500 experiments in total across three models and nine biases (abstract). Per-bias percentages not extracted this session.
limits: Only abstract and introduction read; no per-bias numbers verified.
agent_relevance: Adds weight to the point that consistency, not just accuracy, separates models on bias items (see c07).

source: Araya (2025) Do Chains-of-Thoughts of LLMs Suffer from Hallucinations, Cognitive Biases, or Phobias in Bayesian Reasoning?
finding: On Bayesian base-rate puzzles, reasoning LLMs did not choose natural frequencies on their own (the format that helps humans). When a prompt told them to, they used it only some of the time and sometimes got the arithmetic wrong.
numbers: Qualitative case study of a small set of reasoning traces (several models including DeepSeek); no accuracy table. One case: model applied natural frequencies superficially and ended with an invalid 50% answer.
quote: They show persistent biases towards symbolic reasoning and avoidance or phobia of ecologically valid strategies.
limits: Few items, no statistics, education-oriented paper. Not a controlled comparison.
agent_relevance: Natural-frequency recoding is a known human debiaser, but models do not apply it by themselves. If we want it, code should do the recoding of probabilities into counts, not ask the model.

source: Scholten et al. (2024) Metacognitive Myopia in Large Language Models
finding: Theory paper: LLMs show five symptoms caused by biased samples in their information environment, including neglect of base rates in conditional computation and neglect of sample size. Proposes monitoring and control, for instance hidden parallel reasoning histories, to approximate metacognition.
numbers: No new experiment numbers; reviews other studies.
limits: Conceptual framework; the proposed fixes are untested here.
agent_relevance: Gives a mechanism claim (models track frequency in the context, not validity or sample size). Fits putting counts and sample sizes into the input in explicit form.

source: Hagendorff et al. (2023) Thinking Fast and Slow in LLMs, versus Binz and Schulz (2022): scaling reversal
finding: Reading c01 and c05 together: classic-trap errors in LLMs first rise with scale (davinci 70% to 90% intuitive on CRT, above the human 55%), then fall to near zero with instruction tuning and chain of thought (ChatGPT-4 0%). Anchoring (c12, c14) does not follow this reversal.
numbers: CRT intuitive-error rate: humans 55%, davinci-003 80%, ChatGPT-3.5 15%, ChatGPT-4 0%. Anchored ratio at top reasoning model still 22% to 25% (c12).
limits: Cross-paper comparison of different task families.
agent_relevance: Reasoning-trap bias and cue-contamination bias have different causes. Fixing one with a stronger model does not fix the other; keep S1 hygiene regardless of model strength.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) BiasBuster (sequential anchoring and primacy)
finding: Anchoring was measured as the distance between the model's overall admission rate and its decision pattern for students shown in different positions of a sequence. GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 showed sequence effects; awareness prompts moderately helped Llama but few-shot examples caused failure.
numbers: Normalised Euclidean distance d in Table 3: GPT-3.5 baseline 0.105, awareness 0.270, contrastive 0.258, counterfactual 0.362; GPT-4 baseline 0.317, selfhelp 0.250. (Direction of 'better' is read from the paper's note that most mitigations improve; sign convention not fully verified.)
limits: Sign convention of d is ambiguous in the extracted table. Treat as weak.
agent_relevance: Earlier decisions in the same context shape later ones: another reason to isolate each attempt in its own fresh context.

source: Wang et al. (2024) REHEAT (reasoning versus answer correctness)
finding: Human grading of chain-of-thought text showed models often reason from a stereotype instead of the stated facts. GPT-4 more often reasoned correctly but gave a cautious non-answer; LLaMA more often got a correct answer from wrong reasoning. Gender-related stereotype items were answered more carefully than neutral counter-intuitive items.
numbers: Four-way split of reasoning versus outcome correctness for GPT-4 and LLaMA2-70B (Figure 4, Table 11); counts not extracted. Gender-stereotype items showed higher accuracy than non-gender counter-intuitive item (Tables 25 to 27).
limits: Small number of hand-graded examples; speculative explanation (alignment training).
agent_relevance: Right answer with wrong reasoning, and vice versa, is common. Supports G10: grade the answer by checks, not by the reasoning story.

source: Itzhak et al. (2024) Instruction tuning and RLHF effects on cognitive biases, as relayed by Sumita et al. (2024) and Malberg et al. (2025)
finding: Relayed claim: instruction tuning and RLHF change the strength of decoy, certainty and belief biases in models. Source paper not opened this session.
numbers: none verified
limits: Secondhand; description appears in related-work text of c19 only.
agent_relevance: Reason to re-test any bias result after a model version change. Open the source before relying on it.

source: Kahneman-style dual-process framing applied to LLMs by Hagendorff et al. and Huang et al.: reasoning as System 2 analogue
finding: Analysis of DeepSeek-R1 reasoning traces: questions with mild anchoring tended to have fewer explicit mentions of the anchor in the reasoning, and the share of anchor mentions fell as reasoning went on, so other context diluted the anchor. Authors use this to explain why longer reasoning reduces anchoring.
numbers: Anchored ratios in c12; trace-mention proportions shown in Figure 3 (values not extracted).
limits: Correlational; reasoning trace may not reflect the real cause (see G10).
agent_relevance: Weak support for letting the model reason before answering when a cue cannot be removed; but G10 warns the trace is not proof. Prefer removing the cue.
